text:
Closest generic prior: [CL4SRec](https://arxiv.org/html/2010.14395v2) constructs contrastive views using random contiguous cropping, item masking and local reordering. These establish context perturbation as prior art, but do not specifically protect recent interactions. [TiCoSeRec](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/download/25540/25312) selects augmentations using timestamp gaps: Ti-Crop retains a fixed-length subsequence with minimum interval standard deviation; Ti-Mask deletes items selected by small adjacent intervals. Its operator ablations compare temporal selection against random counterparts. Temporal uniformity differs from recency protection: either can retain older interactions.

A closer recency precedent is [IeSRec, published August 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44443-026-01197-1), which explicitly deletes items starting from the oldest end to emphasize recent behavior. Therefore, protecting recent context should not be presented as broadly novel. For BERT4Rec-family context, [CBiT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.03895) combines cloze masking and dropout to generate contrastive views. Separately, [Is Contrastive Learning Necessary?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.11136) finds that direct augmentation can match or outperform some contrastive methods, motivating an augmentation-only control.

Recommended controls—not established findings: compare unchanged BERT4Rec, uniform random deletion, deletion restricted to older history with a protected recent suffix, and oldest-prefix cropping. Match the exact number of removed interactions per example, target positions, training updates and masking policy; sweep suffix protection while holding deletion count fixed. Add recent-only deletion as a directional control. Keep deletion distinct from reserved-token masking, and control position reassignment after compaction. Improvement over matched uniform deletion would support selective recency protection beyond generic regularization; comparison with prefix cropping tests whether scattered historical retention contributes.
